entry.title: Where did Halloween come from? | Harvard Explains

media:group.media:title: Where did Halloween come from? | Harvard Explains
media:group.media:description: Have you ever wondered where trick-or-treating came from? Or why we carve spooky faces into pumpkins? The origins of both practices, and Halloween itself, come from the Celtic festival of Samhain. Ciara Ní Riain, lecturer at Harvard University's Department of Celtic Languages & Literatures, tells the story of how the ancient Irish festival morphed into what we now know as Halloween.

entry.title: Harvard Thinking: Who should take GLP-1s?

media:group.media:title: Harvard Thinking: Who should take GLP-1s?
media:group.media:description: GLP-1 usage has surged as a weight loss management drug. But given how new they are to the market, medical professionals are only now starting to figure out who should – and should not – be using them. In this episode, host Samantha Laine Perfas talks with obesity specialist Caroline Apovian, evolutionary biologist Daniel Lieberman, and obesity medicine physician scientist Fatima Cody Stanford about why we should be excited – and cautious – about the potential of GLP-1s.

entry.title: Harvard Thinking: Is your parenting style working?

media:group.media:title: Harvard Thinking: Is your parenting style working?
media:group.media:description: Children have minds of their own and those minds might lead to behaviors parents either want to mitigate or reinforce. Parents have difficult choices to make when it comes to guiding their kids, all with the goal of raising successful human beings. In this episode, host Samantha Laine Perfas talks with economist Emily Oster, clinical psychologist Meredith Elkins, and educator Kiran Bhai about how to tell if your parenting tactics are helping or hurting your kid’s development.

entry.title: What Sea Urchins Can Teach Us About Healthy Aging

media:group.media:title: What Sea Urchins Can Teach Us About Healthy Aging
media:group.media:description:
Andrea Bodnar studies what sea urchins can teach us about healthy aging. As science director at the Gloucester Marine Genomics Institute (GMGI), she compares species that live only a few years with others that can live for more than 200. Sea urchins and humans share many of the same cellular processes, and understanding how these animals maintain their health could help researchers identify new targets for drugs to treat age-related diseases and cancer.
GMGI is a nonprofit research institute on Gloucester’s waterfront. Its co-founders include Harvard Medical School professors David Walt and Marc Vidal and former Harvard professor Greg Verdine. Harvard faculty also serve on its science advisory board, helping guide research into ocean life and what it can teach us about ourselves.

entry.title: Harvard Thinking: The healing power of gene therapy

media:group.media:title: Harvard Thinking: The healing power of gene therapy
media:group.media:description: Gene therapy has been used to treat many previously incurable conditions, like correcting deadly genetic disorders or giving children born with hearing loss the ability to hear. The field has massive potential, but there are still many economic, regulatory, and scientific hurdles to overcome to adequately address a variety of both rare and more common conditions. In this episode, host Samantha Laine Perfas talks with gene editing researcher David Liu and ear, nose, and throat surgeon Eliot Shearer about how gene therapy can help treat diseases that were previously considered too rare to research.

media:group.media:title: Welcome to Harvard, Class of 2030!
media:group.media:description: As Harvard’s Class of 2030 arrived in Harvard Yard for move-in day, students shared what they’re looking forward to, from meeting new people to starting classes to exploring campus, while their parents talked about their own mixed emotions. They shared feeling both pride and sadness that comes with the day, and the start of a new chapter—for everyone.
